title: Knowing Stuff is Inseparable from Literacy
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart argues that his Non-Freaked Out Framework for literacy instruction quietly assumes a knowledge-rich curriculum, and that skills-only readings of the Common Core are mistaken. Drawing on Hirsch and Pondiscio's point that comprehension is domain specific, he shows that a reader lacking background knowledge is not a poor reader but an uninformed one. He then attacks the Guide on the Side versus Sage on the Stage dichotomy as false, insisting that great teachers move between both roles. The case is made through the baseball double-play example, a food-sharing analogy, and a closing story about his kindergartener learning about animals. The move is to reframe content knowledge as the engine of reading skill rather than its rival, with the Googleability of facts offered no escape from that.
points: Reading comprehension depends on domain-specific background knowledge, so a student who cannot understand a text may lack knowledge rather than reading skill.
The Common Core era's slogan that skills matter more than content is called fallacious; great teaching must attend to both.
The Guide on the Side versus Sage on the Stage choice is a false dichotomy; the best teachers judge when to work from each place.
Teachers should aim to shrink the knowledge advantage they hold over students by graduation, since brains full of information can do what empty ones cannot, Google or no Google.
A kindergartener's animal knowledge makes her later reading about animals richer, illustrating a loop in which knowledge builds reading and reading builds knowledge.
quotes: Unless we have background knowledge about what we're reading, we won't be able to read it at all — we'll simply decode weird words [2].

If you've never heard of A-Rod or a 6-4-3 double play and cannot reconstruct the game situation, you are not a poor reader. You merely lack the domain-specific knowledge of baseball to fill in the gaps.
This simple fact — that knowing stuff is inseparable from being able to read stuff — is why great teaching will always be concerned with both skills and content.
But it's not true; you can't be literate without knowing stuff, and the Googleability of seemingly everything doesn't change that.

The “Guide on the Side” versus “Sage on the Stage” dichotomy is false; it dangerously oversimplifies the complex truth that the best teachers serve as both sage and guide, possessing the wisdom to decide when to work from either place.
Brains filled with information can do things that brains empty of it can't, Google or no Google.

She won't simply decode the words in books on giraffes or monkeys or dolphins, she'll comprehend them. She'll build knowledge through reading, which will in turn make her better able to build more knowledge through reading, and all the while she'll be becoming a much stronger reader.
